ai-8171b9214e.headline: Meta's new frontier model Muse Wonder Full breaks into the AI top tier
ai-8171b9214e.fulltext:
Meta's new frontier model Muse Wonder Full breaks into the AI top tier
Key Points
- Meta's two new models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, close the gap to the leading frontier models.
- The biggest gains are in agentic coding and autonomous problem-solving.
- Both versions cost nearly three times as much per API call as their predecessor, Muse Spark 1.3.
Meta released its frontier model Muse Wonder in two variants, and both land among the best AI models available.
Muse Wonder Full scores 56 points on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3, while Muse Wonder hits 52. Its predecessor, Muse Spark 1.3, sat at 48 points, which makes this a significant jump from what was a mid-tier model.
The biggest gains show up in agentic evaluations, tests that measure how well an AI model can handle complex tasks on its own. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, performance jumped from 33 to 57 percent. Muse Wonder Full places in the top three on six out of ten benchmarks overall, a strong result for Meta, which seems to have recovered after a weaker stretch with its open Llama models.
Meta highlights two new features. "Active Memory" lets the model remember key information across conversations and recall it when needed. "Active Focus" is the model's ability to stick with difficult tasks, try alternative approaches, and ask follow-up questions when something isn't clear. Both are central to Meta's pitch for a personal AI agent that can access calendars, messages, and documents.
Both models support a one-million-token context window and accept text, images, video, and audio as input. Muse Wonder is available through Meta's API and Muse Code, while Muse Wonder Full is currently limited to Muse Code users. Muse Wonder will soon power the Muse app as well, starting with paying subscribers. Over time, Meta plans to build specialized models from it for all users.
Coding jumps sharply, but factual knowledge lags behind
Both models show big improvements in coding. Muse Wonder Full hits 68 points on the Coding Agents Index, tying Claude Code with Sonnet 5.5. Muse Wonder scores 63, up from 54 for its predecessor.
Factual knowledge remains a weak spot. On the AA-Omniscience knowledge test, Muse Wonder Full manages only 30 points, and Muse Wonder gets 25. That's well behind Claude Opus 5.5 (46), GPT-6 Astra (43), and Gemini 4 Argon (42), which suggests the Wonder series is built on a smaller base model than its competitors. Low hallucination rates help offset this gap. Muse Wonder Full cuts its hallucination rate from 33 to 23 percent compared to its predecessor, the second-lowest among all models scoring at least 45 index points. Only Gemini 4 Argon (15 percent) hallucinates less often.
Meta addresses a common criticism in its blog post, that Muse models are tuned for benchmarks but fall short in real-world use. The company says Muse Wonder Full does better than expected on unfamiliar tasks that weren't part of training optimization, and credits this to a stronger base model.
On the Vals AI Index, Muse Wonder Full (Max) debuts at fifth place and beats all OpenAI models, according to Vals AI. Only current Anthropic models score higher. Muse Wonder lands at tenth.
The biggest improvements come from coding and math. On ProofBench, a private benchmark for mathematical proofs, Muse Wonder Full solves 94 out of 100 problems, up from 58 for its predecessor. That puts it just five to six points behind the top models (99 to 100). On Terminal-Bench 4, Muse Wonder Full doubled its score while using 30 percent fewer output tokens. Performance on finance and legal tasks stayed at predecessor levels, dropping up to two points.
Better performance comes at a steep price
According to Artificial Analysis, Muse Wonder runs $4.52 per task on the Intelligence Index, nearly three times more than Muse Spark 1.3 ($1.60). Token pricing has climbed too, with $4 per million input tokens and $20 for output, up from $1.25 and $4.25 for the predecessor. Muse Wonder also uses 28 percent more input tokens per task, and those account for 76 percent of total costs.
That puts Muse Wonder below Claude Fable 5.1 ($7.63) and Claude Opus 5.5 ($5.98) in pricing, but above GPT-6 Astra ($3.26), Gemini 4 Argon ($1.99), and GPT-6.1 Sol ($0.72). No token pricing is available yet for Muse Wonder Full. Both models do use about 10 percent fewer output tokens than their predecessor.
Meta says it trained the models at its in-house Prometheus data center at gigawatt scale. More details are in the model card.

ai-c511baafb2.headline: Chip Stocks Fall As Broadcom, Intel CEOs Warn About AI Funding
ai-c511baafb2.fulltext:
Chip stocks dropped on Monday as investors weighed comments by the chief executives of Broadcom (AVGO) and Intel (INTC), who warned that access to financing could be a major constraint on the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout.
Speaking at the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference in Singapore on Monday, Broadcom CEO Hock Tan said financing issues could become a bigger obstacle to AI expansion than shortages of processors, memory chips or electricity, CNBC reported.
Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan echoed those concerns, noting rising borrowing costs. He also raised questions about the return on investment for AI.
"If there's any challenge in the front, it's capital and the cost of capital, and then the other part is, in the longer run, people want to see the ROI," he said.
Despite concerns about financing, both executives remained bullish on near-term demand for AI computing infrastructure.
But the comments from the executives sent a chill across chip stocks. The Philadelphia semiconductor index, known as SOX, dropped for the fourth consecutive session. On the stock market today, the SOX fell 2.7%.
The SOX includes the 30 largest chip stocks traded in the U.S., including Broadcom and Intel.
On Monday, Broadcom stock slid 1.9% to 354.73. Intel stock retreated 3.2% to close at 101.35.
At the DBS conference, Broadcom's Tan compared many AI investors to casino gamblers. He suggested that some have little understanding of what they're betting on, Bloomberg reported.
"A lot of investors have no clue what they are investing in," he said. They "set very extreme expectations only to find out that it's almost like they are in a casino."

india-1703d99520.headline: India’s retail inflation jumps to 5.54% in September, above estimates
india-1703d99520.fulltext:
India's headline inflation rose to 5.54% in September from 4.82% in August, adding pressure on the country's central bank to further tighten monetary policy.
The consumer price index print was slightly above economists' expectations of 5.40%, according to a Reuters poll. Inflation has been on the rise for 11 straight months in the world's fastest-growing economy and has touched a 22-month high in September.
India's food inflation climbed 7.74% in September from 5.97% the month prior, with prices rising faster in rural areas than cities, India's Ministry of Statistics and Program Implementation said in a Monday release. Transport services for goods inflation rose 14.73% while that for personal transport jumped 7.46%, as per the release.
Earlier this month, the Reserve Bank of India raised its interest rates for the first time since 2023, joining several major central banks in tightening monetary policy in a bid to arrest accelerating inflation. India's central bank also said that in the "current conditions" further rate cuts were "off the table in the near term" and policy action could either be a rate hike or a pause.
Inflation risks mount
India is among the countries most vulnerable to the supply disruptions caused by the Iran war. It imports nearly 85% of its fuel needs, and before the Iran war it heavily relied on energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz.
Oil prices have been elevated due to the tensions in the Middle East. Experts, however, predict that prices will remain volatile in the near term amid concerns over the Middle East conflict and the impact of Hurricane Isaias.
India's central bank expects core inflation to be at 4.4% for the financial year ending March 2027 and headline inflation at 5.2%, which is higher than the RBI's medium-term target of 4%.
The RBI raised India's economic growth estimate by 40 basis points to 7.1% but cautioned that protracted geopolitical tensions, trade frictions, tightening of financial conditions and elevated international commodity prices would likely weigh on economic activity.
Food prices in particular and India's rural economy also face an added risk from the Super El Nino, with the country receiving its lowest rainfall in over a decade during June to September, a key season for its largely rain-fed farms and reservoirs.
The rainfall was the fourth lowest since 2001, and the 13th driest since 1901, according to the India Meteorological Department. Several parts of key farm states such as Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Punjab, and Haryana are facing extreme drought conditions.
HSBC said in a report on Oct. 7 that it expects another rate hike in December, a day after the RBI policy action. "This may not be a deep tightening cycle, but a tightening cycle it is," the analysts said, adding that the September retail inflation data is likely to show a "sizeable headline pop."

indian-startups-039dce740e.headline: Hero Electronix-Owned Tessolve Secures $75 Mn To Expand Semiconductor Capabilities
indian-startups-039dce740e.fulltext: Hero Electronix-owned Tessolve Semiconductor raised $75 Mn (₹718 Cr) in a funding round led by Vector Line Capital, with additional participation from existing backers TPG and Novo Tellus Capital Partners. The fresh capital will support acquisitions that complement its existing capabilities, broaden its service offerings and strengthen its international business. The company is already in advanced discussions to close multiple acquisitions over the next couple of quarters. It last acquired Germany's Dream Chip Technologies GmbH (DCT) in a ₹400 Cr deal back in November 2024. “This investment will support acquisitions that further strengthen our offerings, and Vector Line’s focus on the sector and their relationships will add significant value,” Tessolve cofounder and chief executive Srini Chinamilli said. Founded in 2004 by Chinamilli, P Raja Manickam and Veerappan V, Tessolve provides end-to-end semiconductor engineering services, spanning chip architecture and design, validation, testing and embedded systems. The company is designing AI and HPC chips by leveraging its in-house pre-engineered semiconductor platforms and design flows to shorten development cycles, alongside a global lab infrastructure and partnerships with leading foundries, IP, EDA and test equipment companies. Tessolve claims to have worked with leading hyperscalers and 18 of the world’s top 20 semiconductor companies. Hero Electronix, the electronics and tech arm of Hero Group, acquired a controlling stake in the semiconductor company in 2016, with plans to complete a phased acquisition of a significant majority holding by the end of that year. “Two decades ago we started with silicon test engineering. Today we are designing and productising complete chips for the companies building AI infrastructure,” Chinamilli said. Tessolve last raised $150 Mn in a fresh round in 2025, led by TPG Growth. With the latest infusion, the startup’s cumulative funding stands at $265 Mn. The development comes amid broader momentum in India’s deeptech sector, where semiconductor and chip design startups have drawn rising investor interest. This increasing investor interest is also supported by the government’s ₹1.25 Lakh Cr India Semiconductor Mission 2.0, which was launched with an aim to build the country’s chip design and manufacturing ecosystem. Some examples of this include AI-native semiconductor verification startup VerifAIX’s $5 Mn seed funding round in September, HrdWyr $13 Mn Series A funding round, among others. Broader investor interest for advanced hardware and tech startups in India, which includes robotics, semiconductors and aerial vehicles, rose 176% YoY to $290 Mn, as per Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report Q3 2026.

india-e10cb8ae68.headline: Indian opposition figures lead march to police barricades around supreme court
india-e10cb8ae68.fulltext:
Delhi police have again obstructed protests in India’s capital as thousands of people returned to the streets, led by opposition leaders, to demand the resignation of the election commissioner.
After mass unrest in the capital over the weekend, when thousands were detained and harassed by police as they attempted to take part in a protest led by the gen Z Cockroach movement, on Monday the main opposition leaders led another procession through Delhi, this time to the supreme court.
The leader of India’s opposition alliance, Rahul Gandhi, alongside other opposition figures and student groups, had declared their intention to march to the court and submit a petition calling for India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to step down.
Kumar has become a deeply controversial figure for his role in an exercise to verify and “purify” India’s electoral rolls, which has led to more than 130m names – more than the population of Japan – being deleted from voter lists since last year.
Opposition parties and civil society groups allege Kumar implemented this special intensive revision (SIR) to help entrench the power of Narendra Modi’s government and his Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Muslim voters and other minorities who are traditionally not BJP voters have allegedly been disproportionately affected by the deletions.
The election commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters could re-enrol, while the BJP has accused its rivals of trying to undermine democracy by questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Several metro stations were closed on Monday in central Delhi and police barricades prevented thousands of protesters getting within 600m of the supreme court, forcing them to turn back.
However, lawyers confirmed they had submitted the petition on Gandhi’s behalf and by late evening, Gandhi had broken through the barricades and reached the court gates.
In a press conference before the march, Gandhi reiterated his allegation that the Modi government was using the commission to commit “vote chori” (cheating) and accused Kumar of being a “thief”.
Gandhi expressed support for the mass uprising of young people, led by the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) and student groups, who had tried to protest over the weekend but were met with police brutality and mass detentions.
“Till the constitution is upheld, till the chief election commissioner is removed, till the system of elections is revamped, till justice is served for India, the youth won’t stop,” he said.
The SIR and calls for Kumar’s resignation have galvanised support for beleaguered opposition parties, who are seen to have flailed in the face of the BJP’s electoral power. Gandhi was detained twice last week after the police refused to let him and other opposition leaders reach Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in central Delhi.
Mahua Moitra, an opposition MP who was marching after being detained last week, alleged that in her constituency in West Bengal more than 10,000 voters had been unjustly removed from the electoral rolls.
“There’s no going back now. People know that their votes have been stolen and this government is finished,” Moitra said. “The police can detain us, they can use brute force and crack our skulls, but we are not going to get off the streets until Gyanesh Kumar resigns and this government is gone. If we don’t stand up to this, then there will be nothing left of our country.”
Moitra accused the supreme court of helping to validate the SIR process and disenfranchise millions of Indians. “When the history of this dark chapter of India is written, the supreme court will be the most disgraced,” she said. “It was the supreme court who put a stamp of approval on every illegality of this government.”
Gandhi has spent months accusing the BJP of fraudulently influencing elections, but his claims have been largely ignored. The issue exploded last month after the Indian Express newspaper reported multiple irregularities in the SIR process that had been pushed through by Kumar.
The protests are likely to continue this week. On Monday, leaders of the CJP approached the Delhi police to seek a date to be allowed to hold a protest without obstruction. They said that if the police refused to comply, their supporters would take to the streets again.

India’s record renewable power generation and solar output were overshadowed by curtailments in July and August when India experienced power availability shortages.
Over 4% of the solar power generated in July and August had to be curtailed because of grid and operational constraints, the Finland-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) said in a report on Monday.
Solar power generation accounted for 58% of the increase in renewable electricity generation in the second quarter of India’s 2026/2027 fiscal year, making it the primary driver of renewable generation growth, CREA’s analysis showed.
“Solar remained the fastest-growing major source of electricity generation in Q2, increasing by 39% year-on-year, compared with 29% for wind and 26% for nuclear,” CREA said. Meanwhile, hydropower generation declined by 20%.
Solar output again reached a new daily record, with 705 million units (MU) generated on September 30, surpassing the previous record in Q1 FY2026-27.
“Despite record renewable generation, significant volumes of renewable electricity continued to be curtailed because of grid and operational constraints,” CREA’s analysts said.
In July and August, about 1.835 billion units (MU) of renewable energy generation, mostly solar, was curtailed, they noted.
Coal and lignite installations were at 231 GW as of August, or a 42% share of all power capacity, but renewable energy (excluding large hydro) grew the fastest, rising to 243 GW, or to a 44% share of India’s capacity, in August 2026. That’s up from 193 GW, or a 39% share, in August 2025, CREA’s analysis showed.
The solar curtailments came as India’s demand surged between July and September and coal plants were increasingly operating with critically low inventories. The number of plants with coal stocks below 25% of normative requirements rose sharply from 32 on August 22 to as many as 85 plants on October 1, according to CREA.
To address curtailments and a lack of flexibility in renewable energy sources, India plans to introduce, from July 2027 a regulation requiring developers of solar and wind energy projects to have battery storage installed at the sites.

indian-startups-6bbf6efc3f.headline: DeepSeek leads $400 million funding round for ex-Tencent scientist's robot AI startup
indian-startups-6bbf6efc3f.fulltext:
China's low-cost AI lab has mostly built its reputation on open-weight language models. Its investment in Unitree Robotics shows how quickly that strategy is moving toward embodied AI.
DeepSeek's clearest verified robotics move so far is its investment in Unitree Robotics' Shanghai IPO. In August, DeepSeek put 140.8 million yuan into the offering, about $20.8 million. That's according to a stock-exchange filing reported by Reuters. Unitree priced the deal at 150.80 yuan a share and raised about 6.1 billion yuan.
The timing fits a broader capital push. Bloomberg reported on October 6 that DeepSeek was close to securing at least 80 billion yuan, about $12 billion, in a new funding round backed by Tencent and battery giant CATL. That follows DeepSeek closing its first external financing earlier in 2026. The round hadn't been announced as closed, but the fundraising reports show how quickly investor interest has built around a lab that spent its first two years building reputation almost entirely on open-weight language models.
That deal came paired with a procurement pact: Unitree gets priority when buying model-training services and technical solutions from DeepSeek, while DeepSeek gets priority when buying robots or pursuing embodied-AI applications with Unitree. Unitree's 150.80 yuan offering price valued the company near $9 billion, making it the first mainland-listed humanoid robot maker in China.
The problem every humanoid robot company is chasing right now is the same one DeepSeek is approaching through Unitree. It needs a model that can look at an unfamiliar room and reliably turn plain instructions into physical action. Large language models are good at predicting the next word. They are much worse at predicting the next joint angle, and that gap is one of the biggest barriers holding humanoid robots back from general-purpose use.
Chinese humanoid robotics companies are minting unicorns at a pace the rest of the world isn't matching. Robotera raised $200 million in May 2026, Unitree filed a $610 million Shanghai IPO on 335% revenue growth, and China now ships 90% of global humanoid robot units, backed by $20 billion in government subsidies and a manufacturing ecosystem... - humanoid robots in Chinese factories - why China leads humanoid robotics
It also fits a pattern across Hangzhou, the city CNBC has described as China's answer to Silicon Valley for AI and robotics, where DeepSeek, Unitree, and spatial-intelligence company Manycore are part of the same startup cluster. The city's AI cluster has increasingly treated embodied intelligence, not another round of chatbot fine-tuning, as the next real contest.
Frankly, DeepSeek didn't need a robotics bet to stay relevant. Its open-weight models already reshaped how the industry talks about training costs. But as LLM gains become more incremental, physical robots that can actually do useful work offer a new battlefield: one where DeepSeek needs hardware partners such as Unitree.
The US side of the race looks nothing alike
Compare that with how the American humanoid robot field is being financed. Figure AI announced in 2025 that it had exceeded $1 billion in Series C commitments at a $39 billion post-money valuation. That's up from its February 2024 valuation of $2.6 billion, with earlier backers including OpenAI, Nvidia, and Microsoft. Tesla's Optimus has no standalone valuation, but Morgan Stanley has described Tesla as an important enabler in humanoid robotics, while Tesla has said first-generation Optimus production lines are being installed in anticipation of production in 2026. Elon Musk has described $20,000 to $30,000 as a long-term target price, not a confirmed commercial price.
Those are hardware bets backed by Big Tech balance sheets and sovereign-scale venture capital. DeepSeek's Unitree stake is much smaller. But it points the same way: AI model companies want a path from software benchmarks into machines that act in the real world.
Both sides are making the same wager. For the last three years the race that mattered was who builds the best chatbot. Now that's giving way to a race over who builds the best body and brain for a machine that can actually pick things up, walk across a warehouse floor, or fold laundry without supervision. DeepSeek made its name proving a leaner model could compete with OpenAI's. Whether that same discipline translates into motion control and real-world perception is the question its Unitree partnership now has to test.

ai-79192f66d4.headline: Delhi Police spotted with Meta AI glasses during Oct 10 protest, compounding privacy concerns
ai-79192f66d4.fulltext:
During the October 10 march at Jantar Mantar, a Delhi Police official on duty was seen wearing Ray-Ban Meta AI glasses, Indian Express Hindi reported, raising questions about police surveillance and civilian privacy rights.
A MediaNama journalist, who was in the vicinity of the protest site that evening, partially corroborated this.
“I took an autorickshaw to Rajiv Chowk around 5 pm on Saturday, October 10. I noticed two police officials at two separate checkpoints, both within a 10-minute radius of Connaught Place, wearing what appeared to be smart glasses while they were stopping and searching vehicles,” he said, asking not to be named for fear of retribution.
To be sure, Delhi Police also uses smart glasses developed by Maharashtra-based Ajna Tech for surveillance purposes.
Software Freedom Law Center (SFLC) has noted in a statement that such commercially developed wearable technologies that can capture audio, video, or other data threaten the privacy of civilians protesting and exercising their rights.
“The use of Meta smart glasses also indicates the possibility of private companies engaging with law enforcement agencies to enable mass surveillance programs in the absence of public disclosures that provide information on the purpose of deploying them and the safeguards applicable to their deployment,” SFLC said.
Are police personnel given these smart glasses for surveillance or any other purpose? If yes, then why?
If not, can any police personnel wear such smart glasses while on duty? And record people without authorization?
The core privacy issue: Smart glasses are designed to look like ordinary glasses, but they are capable of taking pictures and recording videos. They do not look like cameras, so passers-by would hardly notice if someone is filming them. The wearer can interact with AI hands-free and take photos and videos simply by touching the frames, without the subject knowing about it.
The onus falls entirely on bystanders then to notice the small capture LED in the glass frames that blinks when recording is in progress.
Creators have already documented how the recording light on Meta glasses can be circumvented. Online tutorials and a Wired investigation showed how wearers can obscure or physically remove the LED light altogether, with recording still possible.
However, Meta claims it has since updated the AI glasses to turn off the camera when the recording LED is tampered with.
The bigger problem is that in India, smart glasses are increasingly being used as a tool of mass surveillance.
During the Cockroach Janta Party protests in July, people alleged that Delhi Police used Meta AI glasses to record them without their consent. In fact, former JNU Students’ Union president and CPI(M) leader Aishe Ghosh filed a petition before the Delhi High Court, alleging the police monitored protestors not only during demonstrations, but also while they were eating and resting. It also alleged that the police had threatened to send footage of student demonstrators to their parents and colleges.
In April, students of Lady Shri Ram College alleged that members of the administration used Meta AI glasses to record and intimidate them after they staged a protest over Principal Kanika Ahuja’s appearance in a BJP social media video.
The AI glasses surveillance issue may become more acute, with Reliance Jio planning to introduce JioFrames, a sub-$105 rival to Meta’s smart glasses which are priced at around $42o in India. Lenskart’s smart glasses also have camera and audio recording features.
What does Indian law say about filming without consent? Filming someone without their consent in India is generally legal in public spaces under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution (freedom of speech and expression), but becomes illegal if it violates a person’s Right to Privacy under Article 21 which involves private areas, or is used for harassment, stalking, or voyeurism.
Existing laws offer limited protection when someone is secretly filmed and the footage is then used to harass them.
The Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 do provide a mechanism for removal of harmful content filmed with smart glasses. However, the process can take up to 36 hours and platforms may or may not act on the complaint.
Second, as the developer of the camera-equipped glasses used to record him.
This is one the first legal cases in India testing whether a smart glass manufacturer can be held liable for the harm stemming from their product.
The broader pattern: The discontent with Meta AI smart glasses has been brewing throughout this year.
A US lawsuit in March 2026 named Meta and Luxottica. The suit alleges Meta marketed the glasses as privacy-focused, but did not disclose that contractors would review captured footage, including intimate recordings.
That lawsuit followed a Swedish investigation. It found Meta sent footage from the glasses, some recorded inside users’ homes, to data annotators in Kenya. Kenya’s data regulator opened an investigation after a digital-rights group complained.
Courtrooms have started barring the Meta AI glasses over covert-recording concerns, including in New York and across England and Wales.

indian-startups-ee8f7b3036.headline: Tonbo Imaging’s Rs 852 Cr IPO offers investor exit
indian-startups-ee8f7b3036.fulltext:
The Rs 852 crore all-offer-for-sale IPO comes as falling exports, weaker profits and negative operating cash flow temper growth prospects backed by a sizeable order book.
Tonbo Imaging India will open its Rs 852 crore initial public offering (IPO) on October 15, with a price band of Rs 665-700 per share. The issue comprises 1.22 crore existing shares offered for sale by promoters and investors, with no fresh issue.
At the upper end, the company is valued at approximately Rs 4,010 crore, or about 79 times FY26 profit after tax. The offer closes on October 19, with listing expected on October 23.
The IPO is primarily an exit opportunity for existing shareholders. The largest sellers are CEAQ Technologies Private Limited, offering 49.98 lakh shares, and CEAQ Technologies Pte. Ltd., offering 41.55 lakh shares. Together, they account for about 75.2% of the shares on offer.
Promoters Arvind Kondangi Lakshmikumar, Ankit Kumar and Cecilia D’Souza will sell 11.50 lakh, 5.80 lakh and 2.30 lakh shares, respectively. Other sellers include Vinimaya Advisory LLP, Timothy Guy Mitchell, Artiman Partners and other individual and institutional investors.
The selling reflects an already investor-heavy ownership structure. Before the offer, CEAQ Singapore held 25.47%, CEAQ India 8.73% and HBL Engineering 14.25%. The three promoters collectively held 17.43%. Other notable shareholders included Florintree Flowtech LLP with 5.17%, Amansa Investments with 4.25% and Yali Deeptech Fund I with 4.19%.
If all offered shares are sold, the promoters’ combined stake would fall to approximately 14.01%, CEAQ India would exit its disclosed holding and CEAQ Singapore would retain about 18.22%. These are calculations based on the disclosed holdings and proposed sale quantities, rather than final post-offer figures.
The Bengaluru-based company, incorporated in 2003, develops thermal imaging equipment, tactical sights and integrated defence sensor platforms. Its prospects are supported by demand for indigenous defence technology, but its financial performance remains sensitive to large contracts and delivery schedules.
Revenue from operations increased 9.55% to Rs 469.08 crore in FY25 before falling 22.69% to Rs 362.65 crore in FY26.
The RHP attributes the fall to “delays in the execution of certain international orders due to disruptions arising from the West Asia conflict, as well as the deferment of certain anticipated orders from Fiscal 2026 to Fiscal 2027.”
The firm’s export sales fell 93.42% to Rs 20.21 crore, accounting for 5.57% of operating revenue, against Rs 307.34 crore and 65.52% in FY25. Domestic sales rose 114.89% to Rs 337.47 crore, or 93.06% of operating revenue, but could not offset the export decline.
Profit after tax fell 30.07% to Rs 50.88 crore in FY26, while EBITDA, or earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, declined 24.77% to Rs 104.62 crore. The EBITDA margin eased to 28.85% from 29.65%.
The company’s operating cash flow was negative at Rs 63.22 crore in FY26, following an outflow of Rs 136.12 crore in FY25. The earlier outflow partly reflected payments for intellectual property acquired from CEAQ Singapore, while rising inventory and order timing have affected working capital.
The five largest customers accounted for 53.03% of FY26 revenue, leaving the company exposed to delays or changes in a relatively small number of contracts.
India’s defence exports reached Rs 38,424 crore in FY26, up 62.66% year-on-year, according to the Ministry of Defence. Paras Defence expected its exports to roughly double in FY27 amid heightened geopolitical tensions. These trends may support demand for specialised defence electronics.
Tonbo’s confirmed order book stood at Rs 314.24 crore at June 2026, with another Rs 118.15 crore of orders received between July and September.

indian-startups-bd5677884f.headline: Deeptech Funding Zooms 2.8X YoY In Q3 Despite Tighter Deal Flow
indian-startups-bd5677884f.fulltext: India’s deeptech startups raised substantially more capital in Q3 2026, even as the number of deals edged lower. As per Inc42’s ‘Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, Q3 2026’, deeptech startups raised $290 Mn across 28 deals, compared with $105 Mn across 29 deals in Q3 2025. The 176% YoY increase outpaced the broader startup ecosystem, where funding grew 5% to $2.2 Bn. For context, deeptech startups are the ones that develop advanced technologies and hardware and include innovations across sub-segments like spacetech, robotics, defence technology and semiconductors. Large Spacetech Rounds Drive Deeptech Funding Surge The sharp rise in funding, despite a marginal decline in deal count, points to a concentration of capital in a smaller pool of startups. In this, large spacetech rounds accounted for a significant share of the funding deployed during the quarter, with the startups in the sector netting $130 Mn, accounting for about 45% of deeptech funding in Q3. Six-year-old spacetech startup Pixxel’s $100 Mn round was one of four mega funding rounds recorded during the quarter. The round accounted for over three-fourths of the segment’s total. Sustaining this momentum will require capital to reach beyond a select group of companies. As per a recent report by the Indian Venture and Alternate Capital Association (IVCA), deeptech startups continue to face a funding gap at the Series B and C stages, with few funds equipped to write the larger cheques needed to take technologies from development to commercial scale. IVCA President Rajat Tandon said bridging this gap, deepening domestic limited partner participation, and improving exit pathways will be critical to building globally competitive deeptech companies. “India’s deeptech opportunity is moving from promise to more investible commitments, with an increasingly institutionalised ecosystem play. The growth in capital flowing into deeptech over the past decade reflects the confidence investors have in India’s scientific and technological capabilities. However, taking deeptech startups and entrepreneurs from the laboratory to global scale will require capital that is patient, appropriately structured, and available across the entire growth journey,” he said. Government Push Adds To Deeptech Funding Momentum Bharat Innovation Fund cofounder and partner Ashwin Raguraman attributed some of the recent momentum to the government’s ₹1 Lakh Cr Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund and its wider push to support technology-led businesses. “I attribute (growth in deeptech funding) this quarter and maybe even last quarter predominantly due to the announcement on the government’s deeptech-focused ₹1 Lakh Cr RDI Fund and a fairly solid government push, which is making capital available to VC funds,” Raguraman told Inc42. The RDI Fund aims to catalyse private investment in research-intensive businesses. Its framework includes eligibility requirements for R&D-intensive technologies at technology readiness level (TRL) 4 or above, indicating that they have progressed beyond basic laboratory validation. New investment vehicles also emerged during the quarter. Asiana Fund and JC Capital jointly launched a ₹1,000 Cr deeptech fund, while Transition VC and Accel launched funds to back technology-led businesses. RDI Fund Faces Questions Over Governance However, the extent to which the RDI Fund has influenced investor sentiment remains uncertain. In August, The Indian Express reported that nearly two-thirds of the more than ₹2,000 Cr allocated to deeptech companies under the scheme had gone to firms with links to members of the panel involved in selecting beneficiaries, raising concerns over potential conflicts of interest. Inc42’s Q3 2026 Indian Investor Ranking & Sentiment Survey, which covered 85 institutional investors, found that 52% considered disclosure and recusal safeguards adequate but said visibility remained limited. Another 25% viewed the issue as a governance failure requiring independent oversight, while 14% said such investment ties could be managed through disclosure and recusal. The remaining 9% said it was not a concern, arguing that the focus should remain on company selection. The findings suggest that the availability of government-backed capital is only part of the equation. Transparency in its allocation and the availability of patient capital across funding stages will also shape the sector’s ability to turn promising technologies into globally competitive businesses.

global-economics-15872a3b1a.headline: DHL joins NX Group in race to build semiconductor logistics in India
global-economics-15872a3b1a.fulltext:
The DHL Group, the world’s third-largest logistics company, is building a semiconductor logistics and warehousing facility in Dholera, Gujarat, close to where Tata Electronics is building India’s first pure-play commercial chip fabrication plant to capture a larger share of the country's $310-billion supply chain and logistics industry.
Vikas Anand, managing director of DHL Supply Chain India, said in an interview with Mint that the company will “initially invest approximately ₹50 crore” to set up the facility, which is expected to become operational by August 2027. Following this, it may increase the investment “three or four times by 2030, depending on the expansion plans that we have with our customers”.
It would be the $70-billion German company's first dedicated semiconductor warehouse in India, though it has built and operates select semiconductor raw-material storage units at its warehouses in Gujarat and Assam.
Semiconductor logistics require specialized, highly controlled clean room standards in terms of dust, humidity and temperature levels, electrostatic-proof floors, vibration-free transportation, and high-value security and tracking standards.
The investment will be a part of DHL's €1 billion ( ₹10,700 crore) outlay in India, which the company announced on 13 November 2025. “Out of this corpus, about ₹5,000 crore is earmarked solely for DHL Supply Chain India, from which about 10% will be invested to cater to semiconductors,” Anand added.
Before DHL, Japan’s NX Group signed a partnership on 9 September with India Semiconductor Mission under the Ministry of Electronics and IT (Meity) to develop “semiconductor logistics infrastructure and strengthen supply chains in India".
The semiconductor bets come as Tata Electronics’s 28-nanometre (nm) chip fab is expected to become operational in Dholera in 2027, Mint reported on 11 September 2025.
Long time in the making
While the logistics facility is still in the planning phase, Anand said work on it began two years ago.
“About 5,000 supply chain specialists at DHL Supply Chain globally work in the semiconductor sector. Within the Asia-Pacific, Taiwan, Malaysia and Singapore are particularly strong. For India, two years ago, when Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced the first semiconductor mission, and investments started coming in, we sent a team from India to Taiwan, Malaysia and Singapore to learn how the business is conducted in these markets.”
“When the semiconductor supply chain starts developing, the first requirement is capital equipment to set up the factories. These are highly precise and sensitive machines, equipped with tiltmeters. In India, most trucks use conventional suspension systems, so we invested in air-ride trucks. We imported air suspension systems from the US and modified our trucks to transport this equipment,” he added, explaining the work that the company has already done to set up a semiconductor supply chain in India.
With this, Anand said he does not expect domestic competition in semiconductor logistics due to the specialized investments it needs, but said global competition is a factor that the company will have to take into consideration.
“Until then, Indian logistics companies will take time to learn as we replicate our global learning into India. We have a head start over many Indian companies,” he added.
While being the third-largest global logistics firm, DHL Supply Chain India remains smaller by revenue than at least five Indian rivals in the country’s logistics and supply chain industry—Allcargo Logistics, TVS Supply Chain Solutions, Delhivery, Mahindra Logistics and Safexpress.
As of fiscal year 2024-25 (FY25), the latest available fiscal filing, DHL Supply Chain India reported ₹2,085.3 crore in operating revenue and a net loss of ₹4.5 crore, according to ministry of corporate affairs filings accessed via business intelligence and financial data platform Tofler.
While Anand did not single out a revenue target from its semiconductor business alone, he said that businesses including semiconductors, data centres, electric vehicles, batteries, solar panels and other clean-energy sectors may contribute about 20% of DHL’s revenue by 2030.
Promising segment
Industry stakeholders backed DHL’s semiconductor bet, underscoring that New Delhi's growing interest in chips will only expand business opportunities for logistics and supply chain support.
“For suppliers, fabs are attractive because they provide long-term contracts, higher gross margins compared with commodity customers and provide ramp-up runways when fabs expand capacity. For logistics, the biggest opportunity may be during equipment installation, since fab equipment requires highly specialized handling,” said Kanishka Chauhan, senior principal analyst at Gartner.
The need for suppliers to be located close to fabs could also drive the formation of semiconductor clusters around manufacturing centres such as Dholera.
“For most industries, being away from a supplier is inconvenient; for semiconductor manufacturing, it can impact uptime and profitability,” Chauhan said. “A semiconductor fab can face heavy losses if production stops unexpectedly. A single interruption in the supply of ultra-high-purity gases and speciality chemicals can halt production. This is why semiconductor ecosystems tend to cluster geographically.”

global-economics-e561be3b27.headline: JPMorgan, Goldman Curb Exposure on $5 Billion Volta AI Loan Sale
global-economics-e561be3b27.fulltext:
BloombergPublished13 Oct 2026, 12:31 AM IST
(Bloomberg) -- JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Goldman Sachs Group Inc. have taken a rare move to limit their exposure on a $5 billion loan sale for AI startup Volta Infrastructure Holdings Ltd. as investors demand higher yields for risky debt tied to the artificial intelligence boom.
The two banks are leading the loan offering for Volta, a new artificial intelligence cloud company. The banks have underwritten a $1.3 billion term loan for Volta, while a $3.7 billion chip loan is not underwritten by the banks — a move to protect themselves from potential risks, according to people familiar with the deal.
Volta’s debt is being pitched with a yield of about 11%, one of the highest borrowing costs seen in the leveraged loan market that’s become popular for financing AI. Notably, the transaction is unrated, which would typically prevent collateralized loan obligations — the biggest buyers of this type of debt — from purchasing the loans.
Representatives for JPMorgan, Goldman and Volta declined to comment.
Lenders usually provide underwrites on an entire debt package to reassure borrowers that a deal will be financed whether investors buy it or not. While underwriting is a lucrative business for the lenders, and is usually tied to buyouts, it carries the risk of being left on the hook if the debt sells at a lower price than agreed on with the borrower or is not sold at all. Debt commitments for AI deals are more unsual.
Banks are wary of getting stung again like they were in 2022, when markets seized up amid rapid interest-rate hikes, leaving lenders with big losses from the hung debt stuck on their balance sheets.
Navigating Risks
At the same time, funding the AI boom — especially with deals for new or untested companies — has required lenders to adopt less conventional underwriting structures in the leveraged finance market, the people said, asking not to be identified because they’re not authorized to speak publicly. Banks are trying to navigate potential risks and make sure they aren’t caught out, they added.
Volta is among a group of AI companies known as neoclouds, which rent access to chips and other AI infrastructure. The company’s deal will be used to finance a data center complex in Norway that will be managed by Volta Infrastructure in partnership with Bitdeer Technologies Group, a Bitcoin miner that operates data centers. Anthropic PBC has already signed a six-year agreement for compute capacity at the site, Bloomberg previously reported, citing people familiar with the agreement.
The $1.3 billion term loan will be used to make lease payments to Bitdeer to use the data center, Bloomberg previously reported. The $3.7 billion chip loan will be used to purchase about 36,000 graphics processing units, or GPUs, made by Nvidia Corp.
Wall Street has thrown its weight behind the AI build out and deals by neoclouds including CoreWeave Inc., Lambda Inc. and Crusoe Inc. have proven that lenders are happy to finance chip purchases. Those earlier transactions, however, came at lower borrowing costs than Volta’s deal.
Volta was founded earlier this year by Ricard Boada and Sofia Gumuzio, two former executives from Brookfield Asset Management Ltd.’s infrastructure business. The company’s goal is to make it easier for top AI labs and smaller startups to pay for Nvidia’s cutting-edge chips.
Commitments for the deal are due on October 14. JPMorgan had begun sounding out investors on the loan in August, Bloomberg previously reported.

global-economics-f92591a9fb.headline: World Economy Holds Up But Nears Limits of Resilience, IMF Says
global-economics-f92591a9fb.fulltext:
[Text below is The Guardian's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
The International Monetary Fund said global growth should pick up next year with a boost from AI investment, but warned the world economy is nearing the limits of its resilience as the energy squeeze persists and financial risks build.
Growth will accelerate to 3.4% in 2027, the fund said Tuesday in its World Economic Outlook. That’s unchanged from the last update in July, while the forecast for this year was raised slightly to 3.1%.
The global economy “could soon test the limits of resilience”, as emergency oil stocks run low and government budgets become overstretched, the International Monetary Fund has warned.
In its twice-yearly World Economic Outlook, the IMF said global growth had withstood the Middle East conflict better than feared over the past six months.
It said the rerouting of oil supplies away from the strait of Hormuz, and the release of strategic energy stocks, had helped to contain the impact on oil prices from the US-Iran war.
However, it warned that emergency stocks are now depleted, and high debt levels and deficits in many countries could leave governments with little capacity to protect consumers from any future jump in prices.
“Without shoring up supply capacity and replenishing policy buffers, the global economy could soon test the limits of resilience,” it said. “Inventories in energy markets are dwindling and additional geopolitical shocks could still transmit rapidly through prices and supply disruptions.”
The International Energy Agency announced the largest-ever emergency releases of oil stocks on to the market in March this year, and promised to accelerate it after a meeting of oil ministers last month.
But in a sign of the system’s vulnerability, the US strategic petroleum reserve was recently reported to have fallen to its lowest level since 1982.
Last week, Donald Trump agreed a deal with Vladimir Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on US imports of Russian diesel in an attempt to bring down prices at the pumps, which analysts said would have little “meaningful” effect.
The World Economic Report was published on Tuesday in Bangkok, where the IMF and World Bank are holding their annual meetings this week, with finance ministers and central bankers scheduled to attend.
Ahead of the gathering, the IMF managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, urged governments to tighten their belts, amid rising global debt levels. “We cannot keep delaying necessary policy action – you have the tools, now have the wisdom to use them,” she said.
In the report, the IMF revised up its forecast for global economic growth this year marginally, to 3.1% – against 3% in its last update in July. Next year’s forecast is unchanged, at 3.4%.
US growth remains unchanged at 2.3% this year and revised up to the same pace, 2.3%, for 2027 – from 2.2% at the last update.
The IMF predicted GDP growth of 1.3% for the UK this year – up 0.3 percentage points from its most recent update in July – in welcome news for the chancellor, John Healey, who is set to arrive in Bangkok later this week.
However, the IMF also warned that prolonged high oil prices and rising interest rates meant growth was likely to “edge down” in 2027, “as higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weigh on consumption and investment”. It cut its UK growth forecast for next year modestly to 1.2%, from 1.3%.
However, the IMF warned that “risks are skewed to the downside” for the global economy. In particular, it pointed to the threat of “a prolonged stalemate or further escalation in the Middle East”, which would lead to higher energy and food prices.
“Further disruptions to energy infrastructure, cyber-attacks, or extreme weather events could amplify these effects,” the IMF added.
Trump has continued to insist that he could launch another wave of attacks on Iran in the coming weeks, with little sign of a peace agreement being negotiated.
The persistence of elevated oil prices means the spike in inflation is now expected to last longer than previously forecast.
Global inflation is expected to be 4.7% this year – the same level as forecast in July – and to decline to 4.1% in 2027 – up from 4% in the last update.
The IMF urged the world’s central banks not to overreact to short-term jumps in inflation, but to be ready to respond quickly if it appears to be becoming entrenched. “With economic conditions in flux, agility is at a premium,” it said.
As well as fresh turmoil in energy markets, the IMF pointed to the continuing risk to the global economy of an AI-driven market crash.

RBI tightens rupee derivatives rules, widens 20% cash reserve requirement
The move is the latest in a slew of measures announced by the central bank since Saturday aimed at supporting the rupee, which has been falling due to steep oil prices and capital outflows
Listen to This Article
The Reserve Bank of India on Monday tightened rules on rupee non-deliverable derivative contracts, limiting overseas clients to using them only for hedging, and widened a 20% cash reserve requirement to banks' own rupee currency hedges.
The move is the latest in a slew of measures announced by the central bank since Saturday aimed at supporting the rupee, which has been falling due to steep oil prices and capital outflows.
Banks with units in India's International Financial Services Centre and some primary dealers, which until now could offer non-deliverable rupee derivatives to non-resident users for any purpose, can now offer them only for hedging, the RBI said Monday.
Authorised dealers will also be required to maintain a foreign exchange risk reserve for foreign exchange derivative contracts involving the rupee undertaken to hedge the currency risk of their own assets and liabilities.
The reserve applies to all rupee currency contracts in which the authorised dealer buys foreign currency against the rupee, and equals 20% of the rupee equivalent of the notional amount of each contract.

The reserve must be deposited in cash with the RBI daily and kept until the contract ends.
Non-deliverable derivative contracts are settled in cash, usually in dollars, without any rupees changing hands.
Reuters reported earlier on Monday that banks have asked the RBI to scrap the 20% cash deposit for FX derivatives used to hedge current-account exposures and charge a flat fee instead.
The rupee, which had fallen more than 6% this year, jumped 1% on Monday after RBI's weekend announcements.

global-economics-6de40ae8d5.source: Business News Today: Latest Business News, Finance News
global-economics-6de40ae8d5.fulltext:
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has raised India’s growth forecast by 60 basis points to 7 per cent for the current fiscal year, 2026-27 (FY27).
“India’s growth remained robust, underpinned by domestic demand and services, despite higher oil prices,” the multilateral agency said in its latest World Economic Outlook (WEO), released during the annual Fund meeting in Bangkok. “India remains among the fastest-growing major economies, with growth in 2026 (Fiscal Year 2026-27) projected at 7 per cent. This reflects stronger-than-expected momentum, supported by resilient domestic demand and robust services activity,” it said.
Earlier this month, the Reserve Bank of India raised its real GDP growth projection for FY27 to 7.1 per cent from 6.7 per cent. At the same time, the World Bank on Tuesday raised India’s growth forecast for the current fiscal year by 50 basis points to 7.1 per cent. However, it cautioned that growth in the second half of the current fiscal year is likely to slow. Last month, the Asian Development Bank (ADB), the OECD, and other global agencies like S&P and Fitch raised India’s FY27 GDP growth projection to around 7 per cent, boosted by robust June quarter economic activity and resilient domestic demand despite the West Asia conflict. The Paris-based Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) raised its GDP growth forecast by 80 basis points to 7.1 per cent for FY27.
IMF highlights benefits of free trade agreements
IMF emphasised that free trade agreements benefit economies such as India. “Efforts to negotiate or deepen new regional and bilateral trade agreements—such as the EU’s recent trade agreements with India and MERCOSUR (the Southern Common Market) or the United Kingdom’s agreement with India—could lower tariffs and nontariff barriers on traded goods and services among participating economies, facilitate adjustments to recent trade policy changes, and strengthen supply-chain resilience,” it said.
On Monday itself, a Bloomberg Economics report said that India’s free trade agreements (FTAs) already in force, including those agreed with the European Union (EU) and New Zealand, could add about $140 billion to the country’s gross domestic product by 2035, lifting economic output by 1.7 per cent and export volumes by 6.2 per cent. One key assumption is that the agreements with the EU and New Zealand are implemented from 2027.

The Power Grid Corporation of India (POWERGRID) has commissioned a transmission project to evacuate 20 GW of renewable energy in Rajasthan.
The transmission project was commissioned on September 22, 2026, and was officially notified on October 11, 2026.
RECPDCL awarded the project to POWERGRID in 2023, and the project was expected to be completed in 18 months.
The project, initially under the special purpose vehicle POWERGRID Ramgarh II Transmission, was later merged with POWERGRID Vataman Transmission.
The project will be undertaken on a build, own, operate, and transfer basis and includes several critical components, including establishing a new 765/400 kV substation with integrated STATCOM technology in Ramgarh.
It also involves constructing a 765 kV double circuit transmission line and extending associated bays at existing substations in Rajasthan.
Earlier this year, POWERGRID Narela Transmission commissioned the final interstate transmission system to evacuate 8.1 GW of power from solar energy zones in Rajasthan.
The significance of these transmission projects is underscored by the staggering 11.5 GW of renewable energy curtailed in Rajasthan since January 2026, with March alone accounting for 8.3 GW, according to Rajasthan Rajya Vidyut Prasaran Nigam.
According to Mercom’s State of Transmission Infrastructure in India report, India’s transmission infrastructure comprised approximately 509,603 circuit kilometers (ckm) of transmission lines and 1,478 gigavolt-amperes of transformation capacity as of June 2026.
India’s transmission network has grown significantly over the past decade, with transmission line length increasing by 50.8% and transformation capacity more than doubling, rising 111.7% between April 2016 and June 2026.
According to the Central Electricity Authority, India aims to expand its power transmission network by 137,500 ckm of lines and 827,600 MVA of substation capacity, at an estimated cost of ₹7.93 trillion (~$84.33 billion), to support 900 GW of non-fossil fuel capacity by the financial year 2035-36.

agritech-25ecc56fe1.headline: Bad Monsoon, No Safety Net: India’s Farmers Are Running Out Of Relief
agritech-25ecc56fe1.fulltext: As India recovers from the worst monsoon seen in years, and the El Niño continues to intensify, more than half of the country’s geographical area is now facing drought-like conditions. This is bringing deep distress in the rural economy as farm incomes and food prices are under threat.On the other hand, the rural employment programme meant to cushion such shocks is providing fewer jobs.The India Drought Monitor of IIT Gandhinagar said on September 23 that 51.2% of India’s geographical area was “abnormally dry or worse (moderate to exceptional drought)” — up from 46% on September 2. The worst-affected regions were the West, at 82%, followed by the Northeast at 64%, the South at 56% and the North at 46%.The drought has already spread across some of India’s biggest agricultural states. Maharashtra has declared 265 of 358 tehsils drought-hit.Karnataka has identified 177 of 240 taluks, or 73.8%, with the state government warning the number could rise beyond 200. Andhra Pradesh has identified 388 of 688 mandals across 21 districts as moderately or severely hit. Rajasthan has identified 117 of 425 tehsils.This has created a risk for rural India greater than the headline rainfall deficit alone suggests. Crops can be sown and still fail after prolonged dry spells, while depleted soil moisture and reservoirs leave less of a buffer for the months ahead.And unlike during previous El Niño-linked droughts, the rural income cushion is already under pressure.India's rural economy is facing a three-way hit of damaged crops, fewer safety-net jobs and rising prices, with another uncertain harvest ahead.Drought Tests India’s Rural CushionThe rainfall numbers don’t tell the whole story.Between June 1 and September 28, Punjab recorded a 42% rainfall deficit, Bihar 31%, Karnataka 30%, Kerala 27%, Haryana 25%, Andhra Pradesh 24%, Rajasthan 22%, Tamil Nadu 20%, Maharashtra 19% and Telangana 17%. The national deficit was 12%.The rain deficit is, however, not an accurate measure of drought. Punjab and Haryana, for example, had higher rain deficits but extensive irrigation ensured no crop loss. There, farmers are facing delayed procurement, sparking fears of distress sale.Kharif sowing data is similarly misleading. The Agriculture Ministry’s Unified Portal for Agricultural Statistics shows sowing was down just 1.21% from last year. But sowing figures do not capture crops that subsequently wilt after prolonged dry spells or erratic rainfall.What should worry farmers more is inadequate soil moisture and groundwater reserves.The Mahalanobis National Crop Forecast Centre said on September 17 that soil moisture was below the 10-year average in parts of Karnataka, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan, Gujarat, western Madhya Pradesh and northern Bihar.The Central Water Commission’s September 24 report showed water storage at 70.8%, 11.5% below the 10-year average. Eastern and northern regions were particularly weak, with live storage at 50% and 62.7%, respectively.The pattern is uneven. Scanty, delayed or erratic rain and prolonged dry spells have hit some regions, while excess rain, floods and landslides have affected others. Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan has declared drought in five states, including Telangana and Rajasthan, while extreme rain and floods have affected 6.11 lakh hectares of cropland.The full extent of crop losses will become clearer once states complete their assessments.Weaker CushioningPrevious droughts saw the rural job programme scaled up as farm incomes came under pressure. In 2009, when a strong El Niño produced a drought affecting 52% of India’s geographical area, MGNREGS was expanded to provide an income back-up. In 2015, higher allocations and days of work under MGNREGS reached a five-year peak.This time, the employment cushion is moving in the opposite direction.The MGNREGS has been replaced by the VB-G RAM G since July 1. During July-September, just 284 million person-days were created, down from 418 million in the same period last year — a 32% drop.Average days of work provided to households have also fallen sharply, from 43.2 days in FY26 to 17 days in FY27 through September.Ground RealityIf the Reserve Bank of India’s latest report is to be believed, the Indian economy is “decoupled” from monsoon shocks because incomes are becoming less dependent on monsoons.On the ground, the reality seems to be different.Sajal Kulkarni, director of the Centre for People's Collective for Revitalizing Rainfed Agriculture Network, said Maharashtra’s Marathwada and Vidarbha regions face 70-80% crop loss, with overall loss of around 60% across the state. These regions have recorded rainfall deficits of 38% and 27%, respectively.“Farmers are selling goats and sheep in distress as they have run out of cash and the VB-G RAM G work is erratic”, Kulkarni told The Core.Maharashtra had already announced a Rs 36,585 crore loan waiver in July, raising the loan limit from Rs 50,000 to RS 2...

work-careers-04ee65a1c1.fulltext:
India’s Job Market Shows Resilience As Postings Fall 5% YoY: Bain & Company
Entry-level jobs dropped year over year. Postings for junior jobs, representing 95% of all job postings for the quarter, fell 11% year over year, an acceleration from the first quarter’s 6% year-over-year decline.
By :  DC Correspondent
Update: 2026-10-12 16:42 GMT
Bengaluru: Bain & Company, in its latest analysis 'Global Job Market Trends' of global job postings, finds that second-quarter job postings fell year over year across major markets, industries, and functions – even as AI-related roles continued to grow. India was among the markets that fared better, with job postings down 5% year over year, compared with steeper declines across several other major markets. The data points to a two-speed labor market, with broad weakness in many sectors and functions coexisting with continued demand in AI-adjacent roles.
Key takeaways from the analysis are outlined below:
Labor demand remains weak across major markets, although India fared better. France (-40%), Brazil (-39%), and the Netherlands (-33%) suffered the largest year-over-year declines among the top 10 markets tracked, followed by Germany (-27%) and the United States (-23%). India (-5%), Canada (-4%), Japan (-7%), China (-10%), and the UK (-9%) fared better.
Core functions remain under pressure. Most major functions recorded double-digit year-over-year declines, with research, design, and development seeing the largest drop at 37%, followed by sales (-32%), marketing (-32%), strategy and analytics (-27%), IT (-25%), and finance (-24%). Engineering (-7%) and other general and administrative functions (-13%) were relatively more resilient.
Bucking the overall trend, AI hiring grew but remains volatile. AI-related postings totaled roughly 351,000 in Q2 2026, up 60% from Q2 2025 and 12% from Q1 2026. AI-related postings also represented a larger share of total postings than a year earlier, although they remained a small portion of overall demand.
Entry-level jobs dropped year over year. Postings for junior jobs, representing 95% of all job postings for the quarter, fell 11% year over year, an acceleration from the first quarter’s 6% year-over-year decline.
Broad-based hiring remains elusive, but pockets of growth remain. Smaller industry categories recorded strong year-over-year growth, including venture capital and private equity (+47%), capital markets (+26%), computer and network security (+19%), and defense and space (+13%). The data points to continued hiring in targeted capabilities even as more general demand contracts.
As global hiring becomes increasingly selective, India’s relatively modest 5% year-on-year decline in job postings highlights its resilience compared with several major markets. Bain & Company’s analysis also points to a shifting demand landscape, with AI-related job postings rising 60% globally year on year in Q2 2026, even as hiring across several traditional functions remained under pressure. The findings underscore how hiring demand is becoming more concentrated in specific capabilities, making it increasingly important for organisations to align their talent strategies with evolving business and skills requirements.

india-deep-tech-0ad4a4cbed.headline: Hero Electronix's chip design firm Tessolve Semiconductor raises $75 million from Vector Line Capital
india-deep-tech-0ad4a4cbed.fulltext:
Tessolve Semiconductor, a Hero Electronix company, has secured a $75 million funding from US-based Vector Line Capital to support its expansion plans, including strategic acquisitions aimed at strengthening its semiconductor engineering capabilities and global operations.
The company said it is in advanced discussions to complete multiple acquisitions over the next two quarters. The proposed deals are expected to complement its existing capabilities, broaden its services and expand its international presence.
The investment marks Vector Line Capital's first investment in India. The firm, which focuses exclusively on semiconductors and the semiconductor supply chain, joins TPG and Singapore-based Novo Tellus as investors in Tessolve.
The company has not disclosed its valuation following the investment or the size of the stake acquired by Vector Line Capital.
What does Tessolve Semiconductor do?
Founded in 2004, Tessolve provides semiconductor engineering services covering chip architecture, design, validation, testing and embedded systems.
The company, led by co-founder and CEO Srini Chinamilli, develops chips used in AI, high-performance computing (HPC), automotive, data centres and industrial applications.
Its capabilities include the design of complete semiconductor chips, including AI, HPC, and analog and mixed-signal chips.
Tessolve said it works with leading hyperscalers, chip startups, system companies and 18 of the world's top 20 semiconductor companies.
The company employs more than 3,500 engineers across 10 countries and operates nine laboratories globally. It also partners with semiconductor foundries, intellectual property (IP) providers, electronic design automation (EDA) companies and test equipment manufacturers.
Tessolve said it uses in-house semiconductor platforms and design processes to shorten chip development cycles.
What did the company and investors say?
Tessolve co-founder and CEO Srini Chinamilli said the company had evolved from offering silicon test engineering services to designing and developing complete chips for businesses building AI infrastructure.
“This investment will support acquisitions that further strengthen our offerings, and Vector Line’s focus on the sector and their relationships will add significant value,” he said.
Vector Line Capital founder and CEO Geoffrey Baldwin said increasing semiconductor complexity was creating demand for engineering partners capable of supporting different stages of chip development.
“Semiconductors are becoming extremely complex, making them harder to design, validate and test. Leading technology companies are increasingly turning to engineering partners who can carry work across the whole development cycle,” Baldwin said.
Ujjwal Munjal, chairman of Tessolve and founder of Hero Electronix, said the company's growth reflected the ability of India-based engineering businesses to compete internationally.
“Tessolve has shown that an engineering business built from India can compete and lead globally,” he said.
Tessolve's previous funding and expansion in India
The latest investment follows a $150 million funding round from global investment firm TPG in September 2025. Earlier, Singapore-based Novo Tellus Capital Partners invested $40 million in Tessolve in 2021.
Tessolve has also expanded through acquisitions. In November 2024, it acquired Germany-based chip design company Dream Chip Technologies for about Rs 400 crore.
In India, the company is working with emerging semiconductor foundries, outsourced semiconductor assembly and testing (OSAT) companies, and chip startups, providing engineering support across different stages of semiconductor development.
The expansion comes as India seeks to strengthen its domestic semiconductor industry, with investments in chip manufacturing, assembly, testing and design.

Founded in 2004 by Chinamilli, P Raja Manickam and Veerappan V, Tessolve provides end-to-end semiconductor engineering services, spanning chip architecture and design, validation, testing and embedded systems. The company is designing AI and HPC chips by leveraging its in-house pre-engineered semiconductor platforms and design flows to shorten development cycles, alongside a global lab infrastructure and partnerships with leading foundries, IP, EDA and test equipment companies. Tessolve claims to have worked with leading hyperscalers and 18 of the world’s top 20 semiconductor companies. Hero Electronix, the electronics and tech arm of Hero Group, acquired a controlling stake in the semiconductor company in 2016, with plans to complete a phased acquisition of a significant majority holding by the end of that year. “Two decades ago we started with silicon test engineering. Today we are designing and productising complete chips for the companies building AI infrastructure,” Chinamilli said. Tessolve last raised $150 Mn in a fresh round in 2025, led by TPG Growth. With the latest infusion, the startup’s cumulative funding stands at $265 Mn. The development comes amid broader momentum in India’s deeptech sector, where semiconductor and chip design startups have drawn rising investor interest. This increasing investor interest is also supported by the government’s ₹1.25 Lakh Cr India Semiconductor Mission 2.0, which was launched with an aim to build the country’s chip design and manufacturing ecosystem. Some examples of this include AI-native semiconductor verification startup VerifAIX’s $5 Mn seed funding round in September, HrdWyr $13 Mn Series A funding round, among others. Broader investor interest for advanced hardware and tech startups in India, which includes robotics, semiconductors and aerial vehicles, rose 176% YoY to $290 Mn, as per Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report Q3 2026.

world-e10cb8ae68.headline: Indian opposition figures lead march to police barricades around supreme court
world-e10cb8ae68.fulltext:
Delhi police have again obstructed protests in India’s capital as thousands of people returned to the streets, led by opposition leaders, to demand the resignation of the election commissioner.
After mass unrest in the capital over the weekend, when thousands were detained and harassed by police as they attempted to take part in a protest led by the gen Z Cockroach movement, on Monday the main opposition leaders led another procession through Delhi, this time to the supreme court.
The leader of India’s opposition alliance, Rahul Gandhi, alongside other opposition figures and student groups, had declared their intention to march to the court and submit a petition calling for India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, to step down.
Kumar has become a deeply controversial figure for his role in an exercise to verify and “purify” India’s electoral rolls, which has led to more than 130m names – more than the population of Japan – being deleted from voter lists since last year.
Opposition parties and civil society groups allege Kumar implemented this special intensive revision (SIR) to help entrench the power of Narendra Modi’s government and his Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Muslim voters and other minorities who are traditionally not BJP voters have allegedly been disproportionately affected by the deletions.
The election commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters could re-enrol, while the BJP has accused its rivals of trying to undermine democracy by questioning legitimate electoral processes.
Several metro stations were closed on Monday in central Delhi and police barricades prevented thousands of protesters getting within 600m of the supreme court, forcing them to turn back.
However, lawyers confirmed they had submitted the petition on Gandhi’s behalf and by late evening, Gandhi had broken through the barricades and reached the court gates.
In a press conference before the march, Gandhi reiterated his allegation that the Modi government was using the commission to commit “vote chori” (cheating) and accused Kumar of being a “thief”.
Gandhi expressed support for the mass uprising of young people, led by the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) and student groups, who had tried to protest over the weekend but were met with police brutality and mass detentions.
“Till the constitution is upheld, till the chief election commissioner is removed, till the system of elections is revamped, till justice is served for India, the youth won’t stop,” he said.
The SIR and calls for Kumar’s resignation have galvanised support for beleaguered opposition parties, who are seen to have flailed in the face of the BJP’s electoral power. Gandhi was detained twice last week after the police refused to let him and other opposition leaders reach Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in central Delhi.
Mahua Moitra, an opposition MP who was marching after being detained last week, alleged that in her constituency in West Bengal more than 10,000 voters had been unjustly removed from the electoral rolls.
“There’s no going back now. People know that their votes have been stolen and this government is finished,” Moitra said. “The police can detain us, they can use brute force and crack our skulls, but we are not going to get off the streets until Gyanesh Kumar resigns and this government is gone. If we don’t stand up to this, then there will be nothing left of our country.”
Moitra accused the supreme court of helping to validate the SIR process and disenfranchise millions of Indians. “When the history of this dark chapter of India is written, the supreme court will be the most disgraced,” she said. “It was the supreme court who put a stamp of approval on every illegality of this government.”
Gandhi has spent months accusing the BJP of fraudulently influencing elections, but his claims have been largely ignored. The issue exploded last month after the Indian Express newspaper reported multiple irregularities in the SIR process that had been pushed through by Kumar.
The protests are likely to continue this week. On Monday, leaders of the CJP approached the Delhi police to seek a date to be allowed to hold a protest without obstruction. They said that if the police refused to comply, their supporters would take to the streets again.
