global-economics-15d2629c7d.headline: Tonbo Imaging sets ₹852 crore IPO price band, targets ₹4,010 crore valuation
global-economics-15d2629c7d.fulltext:
Tonbo Imaging India, a defence electronics maker, has set a price band of ₹665-700 per share for its ₹852 crore (around $88 million) initial public offering (IPO), showed its red herring prospectus (RHP) filed on Monday.
At the upper end, the company would be valued at around ₹4,010 crore (around $420 million).
The issue is entirely an offer for sale (OFS) of 12.2 million equity shares by promoters and existing investors, with no fresh issue component. This means that there will be no fresh capital infusion into the company.
Promoters Arvind Kondangi Lakshmikumar, Ankit Kumar and Cecilia D’Souza are partially selling their holdings in the company, as part of Tonbo Imaging's promoter group, Vinimaya Advisory LLP.
Other investors who are partially exiting their stakes include Singapore-based CEAQ Technologies, angel investors Timothy Guy Mitchell, Amit Dilip Shah and Ramesh Radhakrishnan. The only investor completely exiting their stake is CEAQ India.
Of the venture capital funds that have invested in the company, only US-based Artiman Partners is partially exiting its stake. The firm was among the first institutional investors in the company when it wrote a $6.4 million cheque in 2012.
Tonbo raised ₹175 crore (around $20 million) in April 2025 from Florintree Advisors, Tenacity Ventures, and Exim Bank. Other investors in the company include Yali Capital, Qualcomm Ventures, and Celesta Capital.
“They’re selling right now because this is a liquidity event to return money to their limited partners,” said Arvind Lakshmikumar, managing director and chief executive of Tonbo Imaging India, in an interview with Mint.
The listing comes as India’s defence sector builds a deep pipeline despite weak ordering in the second quarter of fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27). A September 2026 results preview by Motilal Oswal Financial Services said that the defence acquisition council approvals stood at ₹1.62 trillion in FY27 so far and ₹13 trillion between FY25 and now.
The brokerage also flagged the opening up of missile production to private firms and a simplified export framework that extends licence validity from two years to three. The export framework, in particular, is relevant for Tonbo, which says that about half its revenue comes from exports.
Picking and choosing
Tonbo’s bid-to-win ratio has slipped from 40.91% in FY24 to 35.94% in FY25, 34.35% in FY26, and 14.29% in the three months ended June 2026, according to its RHP. In that quarter, it won two of 14 bids, with five lost and seven still active. Across the period, it submitted 275 bids and won 97.
Lakshmikumar said Tonbo skips mass-market tenders that draw about 10 bidders on diluted specifications, and tries to persuade customers to tighten them beforehand. The RHP says some bids were lost on tenders with loosely defined specifications, and that Tonbo may have to cut prices to win.
“We convince the customer that what they need is a Ferrari, but we get it to them at a price point in between a Ferrari and a Maruti,” he said, adding that Tonbo walks away when even that price is unacceptable.
The approach carries risk. The RHP says contracts are short-term and non-recurring, so Tonbo must keep winning fresh tenders. It received orders worth ₹118.15 crore between July and September 2026.
Lakshmikumar said the company opted not to raise fresh capital through the IPO as it had raised money last year and already has working capital lines and term loans with banks. “Fresh funding can wait for the next year, and after we demonstrate our performance as a public company. Dilution can be reduced, and that's why we chose to do an OFS and not a primary right now."
Diversifying revenue concentration
In its RHP, Tonbo has flagged revenue concentration from its top five customers over the last three fiscals. In FY24, its top five customers contributed to 72% of its revenue; in FY25, that number jumped to 86%. In FY26, it declined to 53%.
In a bid to diversify beyond over-reliance on specific geographies or nations, the company has empanelled itself for defence programmes across 24 countries, according to Lakshmikumar. “…when you are present in many places, you automatically kind of hedge your risks across different geographies.”
Its revenue is also split between exports to developing and developed nations and bidding for tenders here in India. What's more, the company's target market is the developing market, where demand for specialized defence equipment is growing.
“We sell in developed markets to demonstrate technology superiority, take that as a case study to developing markets to show them that it can be done,” said Lakshmikumar. “When we walk into the Philippines, Armenia, Vietnam, and demonstrate that we've sold our products in developed markets, it's a very easy sell.”

india-deep-tech-772d541cbe.headline: Deeptech Funding Zooms 2.8X YoY In Q3 Despite Tighter Deal Flow
india-deep-tech-772d541cbe.fulltext: India’s deeptech startups raised substantially more capital in Q3 2026, even as the number of deals edged lower. As per Inc42’s ‘Indian Tech Startup Funding Report, Q3 2026’, deeptech startups raised $290 Mn across 28 deals, compared with $105 Mn across 29 deals in Q3 2025. The 176% YoY increase outpaced the broader startup ecosystem, where funding grew 5% to $2.2 Bn. For context, deeptech startups are the ones that develop advanced technologies and hardware and include innovations across sub-segments like spacetech, robotics, defence technology and semiconductors. Large Spacetech Rounds Drive Deeptech Funding Surge The sharp rise in funding, despite a marginal decline in deal count, points to a concentration of capital in a smaller pool of startups. In this, large spacetech rounds accounted for a significant share of the funding deployed during the quarter, with the startups in the sector netting $130 Mn, accounting for about 45% of deeptech funding in Q3. Six-year-old spacetech startup Pixxel’s $100 Mn round was one of four mega funding rounds recorded during the quarter. The round accounted for over three-fourths of the segment’s total. Sustaining this momentum will require capital to reach beyond a select group of companies. As per a recent report by the Indian Venture and Alternate Capital Association (IVCA), deeptech startups continue to face a funding gap at the Series B and C stages, with few funds equipped to write the larger cheques needed to take technologies from development to commercial scale. IVCA President Rajat Tandon said bridging this gap, deepening domestic limited partner participation, and improving exit pathways will be critical to building globally competitive deeptech companies. “India’s deeptech opportunity is moving from promise to more investible commitments, with an increasingly institutionalised ecosystem play. The growth in capital flowing into deeptech over the past decade reflects the confidence investors have in India’s scientific and technological capabilities. However, taking deeptech startups and entrepreneurs from the laboratory to global scale will require capital that is patient, appropriately structured, and available across the entire growth journey,” he said. Government Push Adds To Deeptech Funding Momentum Bharat Innovation Fund cofounder and partner Ashwin Raguraman attributed some of the recent momentum to the government’s ₹1 Lakh Cr Research, Development and Innovation (RDI) Fund and its wider push to support technology-led businesses. “I attribute (growth in deeptech funding) this quarter and maybe even last quarter predominantly due to the announcement on the government’s deeptech-focused ₹1 Lakh Cr RDI Fund and a fairly solid government push, which is making capital available to VC funds,” Raguraman told Inc42. The RDI Fund aims to catalyse private investment in research-intensive businesses. Its framework includes eligibility requirements for R&D-intensive technologies at technology readiness level (TRL) 4 or above, indicating that they have progressed beyond basic laboratory validation. New investment vehicles also emerged during the quarter. Asiana Fund and JC Capital jointly launched a ₹1,000 Cr deeptech fund, while Transition VC and Accel launched funds to back technology-led businesses. RDI Fund Faces Questions Over Governance However, the extent to which the RDI Fund has influenced investor sentiment remains uncertain. In August, The Indian Express reported that nearly two-thirds of the more than ₹2,000 Cr allocated to deeptech companies under the scheme had gone to firms with links to members of the panel involved in selecting beneficiaries, raising concerns over potential conflicts of interest. Inc42’s Q3 2026 Indian Investor Ranking & Sentiment Survey, which covered 85 institutional investors, found that 52% considered disclosure and recusal safeguards adequate but said visibility remained limited. Another 25% viewed the issue as a governance failure requiring independent oversight, while 14% said such investment ties could be managed through disclosure and recusal. The remaining 9% said it was not a concern, arguing that the focus should remain on company selection. The findings suggest that the availability of government-backed capital is only part of the equation. Transparency in its allocation and the availability of patient capital across funding stages will also shape the sector’s ability to turn promising technologies into globally competitive businesses.

india-9ce4680cdd.headline: IMF raises India's FY27 growth forecast to 7% from 6.4%, citing resilient domestic demand
india-9ce4680cdd.fulltext:
15
The IMF has raised India's growth outlook by 60 basis points despite higher global energy prices, citing stronger economic momentum, robust services activity and sustained domestic demand
  October 13, 2026 / 07:31 IST  
India's economy is projected to grow 7 percent in FY27, higher than the 6.4 percent estimated earlier, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said in its October World Economic Outlook (WEO), as strong domestic demand and services activity helped the country withstand global economic disruptions.
The upward revision from the July forecast comes despite higher oil prices and continued geopolitical tensions arising from the conflict in the Middle East.
The IMF also raised its FY28 growth forecast to 7 percent from 6.7 percent, suggesting that India's growth momentum could extend beyond the current financial year.
India remains among the fastest-growing major economies, with economic activity performing better than previously expected.
The IMF upgrade follows similar action by other international agencies, as India's growth surprised on the upside in the first quarter with the economy clocking 7.8 percent increase in economic output from last year.
Reserve Bank of India was latest to revise its growth forecast upward to 7.1 percent from 6.7 percent projected earlier.
Domestic demand drives upgrade
The IMF attributed the stronger outlook to resilient domestic demand and robust services activity, which have supported economic growth despite rising energy costs.
India's economy expanded 7.8 percent in FY26, according to the figures presented in the WEO, and growth is projected to moderate to 7 percent in FY27 before remaining at that level in FY28.
The improvement stands out against a more uneven global economic outlook, with the IMF warning that countries face divergent growth prospects depending on their exposure to higher energy prices and their participation in the global technology upturn.
The IMF also identified India's favourable demographic dynamics, large and expanding domestic market, and continued structural reforms as factors supporting its medium-term growth potential.
India stands out amid global slowdown
It expects global economic growth to moderate from 3.5 percent in 2025 to 3.1 percent in 2026, before recovering to 3.4 percent in 2027.
China's growth, meanwhile, is projected to slow from 5 percent in 2025 to 4.5 percent in 2026 and 4 percent in 2027, reflecting higher oil prices, weak domestic demand and continuing structural challenges.
The contrast is particularly significant as several energy-importing emerging economies face downward revisions to their growth outlook.
Inflation and external risks remain
Despite the growth upgrade, India continues to face risks from higher commodity prices and external imbalances.
The IMF projects India's consumer inflation at 5 percent in FY27, compared with 2 percent in FY26, before moderating to 4.4 percent in FY28. India's inflation climbed to 5.5 percent in September, the highest level in new series.
IMF's projection is slightly lower than RBI's estimate of 5.2 percent for FY27.
India's current account deficit is projected to widen to 1.5 percent of GDP in FY27 from 0.7 percent in FY26, before narrowing to 1.3 percent in FY28.
The global outlook remains vulnerable to further disruptions in oil supplies, renewed trade tensions and tighter financial conditions, even as India continues to demonstrate relatively strong growth momentum.

india-25ecc56fe1.headline: Bad Monsoon, No Safety Net: India’s Farmers Are Running Out Of Relief
india-25ecc56fe1.fulltext: As India recovers from the worst monsoon seen in years, and the El Niño continues to intensify, more than half of the country’s geographical area is now facing drought-like conditions. This is bringing deep distress in the rural economy as farm incomes and food prices are under threat.On the other hand, the rural employment programme meant to cushion such shocks is providing fewer jobs.The India Drought Monitor of IIT Gandhinagar said on September 23 that 51.2% of India’s geographical area was “abnormally dry or worse (moderate to exceptional drought)” — up from 46% on September 2. The worst-affected regions were the West, at 82%, followed by the Northeast at 64%, the South at 56% and the North at 46%.The drought has already spread across some of India’s biggest agricultural states. Maharashtra has declared 265 of 358 tehsils drought-hit.Karnataka has identified 177 of 240 taluks, or 73.8%, with the state government warning the number could rise beyond 200. Andhra Pradesh has identified 388 of 688 mandals across 21 districts as moderately or severely hit. Rajasthan has identified 117 of 425 tehsils.This has created a risk for rural India greater than the headline rainfall deficit alone suggests. Crops can be sown and still fail after prolonged dry spells, while depleted soil moisture and reservoirs leave less of a buffer for the months ahead.And unlike during previous El Niño-linked droughts, the rural income cushion is already under pressure.India's rural economy is facing a three-way hit of damaged crops, fewer safety-net jobs and rising prices, with another uncertain harvest ahead.Drought Tests India’s Rural CushionThe rainfall numbers don’t tell the whole story.Between June 1 and September 28, Punjab recorded a 42% rainfall deficit, Bihar 31%, Karnataka 30%, Kerala 27%, Haryana 25%, Andhra Pradesh 24%, Rajasthan 22%, Tamil Nadu 20%, Maharashtra 19% and Telangana 17%. The national deficit was 12%.The rain deficit is, however, not an accurate measure of drought. Punjab and Haryana, for example, had higher rain deficits but extensive irrigation ensured no crop loss. There, farmers are facing delayed procurement, sparking fears of distress sale.Kharif sowing data is similarly misleading. The Agriculture Ministry’s Unified Portal for Agricultural Statistics shows sowing was down just 1.21% from last year. But sowing figures do not capture crops that subsequently wilt after prolonged dry spells or erratic rainfall.What should worry farmers more is inadequate soil moisture and groundwater reserves.The Mahalanobis National Crop Forecast Centre said on September 17 that soil moisture was below the 10-year average in parts of Karnataka, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan, Gujarat, western Madhya Pradesh and northern Bihar.The Central Water Commission’s September 24 report showed water storage at 70.8%, 11.5% below the 10-year average. Eastern and northern regions were particularly weak, with live storage at 50% and 62.7%, respectively.The pattern is uneven. Scanty, delayed or erratic rain and prolonged dry spells have hit some regions, while excess rain, floods and landslides have affected others. Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan has declared drought in five states, including Telangana and Rajasthan, while extreme rain and floods have affected 6.11 lakh hectares of cropland.The full extent of crop losses will become clearer once states complete their assessments.Weaker CushioningPrevious droughts saw the rural job programme scaled up as farm incomes came under pressure. In 2009, when a strong El Niño produced a drought affecting 52% of India’s geographical area, MGNREGS was expanded to provide an income back-up. In 2015, higher allocations and days of work under MGNREGS reached a five-year peak.This time, the employment cushion is moving in the opposite direction.The MGNREGS has been replaced by the VB-G RAM G since July 1. During July-September, just 284 million person-days were created, down from 418 million in the same period last year — a 32% drop.Average days of work provided to households have also fallen sharply, from 43.2 days in FY26 to 17 days in FY27 through September.Ground RealityIf the Reserve Bank of India’s latest report is to be believed, the Indian economy is “decoupled” from monsoon shocks because incomes are becoming less dependent on monsoons.On the ground, the reality seems to be different.Sajal Kulkarni, director of the Centre for People's Collective for Revitalizing Rainfed Agriculture Network, said Maharashtra’s Marathwada and Vidarbha regions face 70-80% crop loss, with overall loss of around 60% across the state. These regions have recorded rainfall deficits of 38% and 27%, respectively.“Farmers are selling goats and sheep in distress as they have run out of cash and the VB-G RAM G work is erratic”, Kulkarni told The Core.Maharashtra had already announced a Rs 36,585 crore loan waiver in July, raising the loan limit from Rs 50,000 to RS 2...

The project, called VIGOR: Moving AI-Discovered Molecules from the Lab to the Clinic, has a total project cost of ₹172 crore (approximately $1.72 billion). The aim is to advance four experimental drugs to technology readiness levels (TRLs) 4 to 6, requiring preclinical development, validation, and preparation for clinical trials. Financial support will be provided through optionally convertible debt (OCD).
Artificial intelligence is opening new possibilities in the field of drug discovery by enabling researchers to identify promising molecules, investigate disease mechanisms, and accelerate the discovery of potential treatments. However, transforming computational discoveries into viable drugs requires extensive experimental validation, preclinical studies, and clinical development.
Peptris’ VIGOR program seeks to address this important shift by leveraging its proprietary AI-powered drug discovery platform to advance a portfolio of molecules toward clinical development. The program focuses on therapeutic areas with significant unmet medical needs and aims to identify and develop novel treatments through a combination of computational capabilities, scientific validation, and established drug-development processes.
The program includes four experimental drugs: PEPR111, which targets neuromuscular disorders and cancer; PEPRX101, which targets hair loss (alopecia); PEPR202, which targets neuropathy; and PEPR112, which targets diabetes mellitus (DMD). Each experimental drug is currently at the TRL-4 stage, and the project aims to advance it to TRL-6. The development program envisages a structured progression over three years, including advanced preclinical and investigational new drug (IND)-enabling studies, formulation development, clinical trial preparation, and initiation activities, subject to relevant scientific and regulatory requirements.
The VIGOR program is designed to accelerate the development of new therapeutic candidates by leveraging Peptris’ AI-based drug discovery capabilities and existing platform experience. This approach combines AI-enabled discovery with established drug development expertise, including the use of a global contract research organization (CRO) network to assist with development and validation. By supporting the progress of multiple candidates under a coordinated program, the project seeks to strengthen the process of translating AI-based research into potential therapeutic products. Its focus on select disease areas also represents an opportunity to direct innovation toward conditions where effective treatment options are limited.
A representative from Peptris Technologies Pvt. Ltd. said, “ The support from TDB under the RDI Fund will help advance our VIROR program and bring AI-discovered molecules to critical preclinical development stages. Our approach combines AI-driven discovery with experimental validation and established drug development processes to address unmet needs in the medical field. This partnership will support our efforts to translate promising computational discoveries into therapeutics that have the potential to move into clinical development. ”
